name: Cyanotype
basis: why: iron-salt paper turns Prussian blue where light strikes; how: blue ramp, coating blotches and brush streaks, ragged pooled edge

lumenary.blurb: A sun print on hand-coated paper: Prussian blue where the light struck, bare paper where it did not, with a brushed edge.

facts.bestOn: Silhouettes, plants and pictures with strong light and shade

why: A cyanotype is a sun print: paper coated with iron salts turns Prussian blue where light strikes it and washes white where it does not. It has no greys other than varying blue. This treatment maps the picture’s brightness onto that chemistry and adds what hand coating always brings: blotches, brush strokes and a ragged edge where the liquid pooled.
how: Stretch the picture, shift it by the exposure slider and add contrast.
Send the result through a five colour ramp from deep blue in the shadows to near white in the highlights. Tea and green toning swap in other ramps.
Change the tone slightly with two noises, one slow and blotchy and one long and thin like a brush stroke.
Stop the coating short of the sheet edge in a ragged line from two more noises, with a darker pooled edge.
Show bare cream paper outside the edge and multiply a fine fibre noise over everything.
history: Sir John Herschel invented the cyanotype in 1842. In 1843 Anna Atkins used it to publish photographic records of seaweeds, often called the first book illustrated with photographs. Engineers later copied their drawings with it, producing the original blueprints, and artists and schoolchildren still make sun prints with the same chemistry.
uses: Blue toned wall art and posters
Cover art with a handmade feel
terms: A deep blue pigment formed in the cyanotype chemistry.
How long and how strongly light strikes the paper.
Changing the colour of a photographic print with a chemical bath.
paragraphs: A cyanotype is made by coating paper with iron salts and exposing it to sunlight; where light strikes, the salts turn Prussian blue, and where it does not they wash away and leave white paper. The treatment maps brightness onto that chemistry. The picture is stretched, shifted by the exposure slider and given contrast; the result runs a five-colour ramp from deep blue (shadows) to near white (highlights). Tea toning and green toning swap in a different ramp.

Hand-coated paper is never even. Two noises, one slow and blotchy, one long and thin like a brush stroke, change the tone slightly (the uneven-coating slider). The coating stops short of the sheet edge in a ragged line made from two more noises, and where the liquid pooled at the boundary the print is darker; outside the edge the bare cream paper shows. A fine fibre noise is multiplied over everything.

equations.note: Tone t: ε is the exposure slider, c the contrast and u the uneven-coating slider.
Colour from the five-stop ramp; c is how coated the pixel is: e the distance to the sheet edge, m = 0.055 of the short side, ρ the ragged-edge noise, σ the picture scale.
Darkening where the liquid pooled along the edge.

presets.text: Tea toning warms the blue into brown.
Overexposure bleaches the print towards white.
Uneven coating with no brushed edge looks more like a full sheet.
